summary: Extends IPv4 multicast addressing so that multicast addresses can be assigned together with unicast prefixes. Operators can then identify their multicast addresses without separate coordination.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines IPv4 multicast addresses based on an organization's unicast address prefix. The prefix identifies the organization, and the remaining bits identify a multicast group.

questions: how does ubm differ from glop
how does the 234/8 multicast range work
subtitle: An IPv4 multicast range derived from an organization's unicast prefix.

tldr.problem: GLOP address allocation is tied to AS numbers, has limits, and does not map directly to organizations' unicast prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses in 234/8 include an organization's global unicast prefix followed by a group ID.
tldr.outcome: The method provides multicast space to organizations with a /24 or shorter prefix and does not replace RFC 3180.

today: RFC 6034 is a Proposed Standard. Its text says it does not obsolete or update RFC 3180, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 6034.

sections.title: Why Use a Unicast Prefix
sections.content:
GLOP assigns multicast space in 233/8 by embedding an AS number, providing 256 multicast addresses per AS. The RFC lists limits: it does not work with four-octet AS numbers, may require other allocation methods within an AS, and gives only 256 automatic addresses.

This document defines a similar-to-IPv6 mechanism for IPv4 based on unicast prefixes. It does not obsolete RFC 3180, which remains needed for allocations more specific than /24.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier method tied multicast addresses to AS numbers and gave a fixed amount per AS. This method ties addresses to the unicast prefix assigned to an organization.

sections.title: The 234/8 Address Layout
sections.content:
An address with prefix 234/8 is a Unicast-Based Multicast address. The remaining 24 bits contain the organization's unicast prefix followed by a group ID. Organizations with a /24 or shorter prefix may use the mechanism; an organization with a longer prefix receives no range from it.

The embedded prefix MUST be a global unicast prefix, and applications MUST NOT hard-code these multicast addresses because global unicast addresses are not permanently assigned. The holder can be identified by shifting the multicast address left by 8 bits and looking up the resulting unicast address.
sections.plainLanguage: The address begins with 234, then carries part of the organization's unicast prefix and a group identifier. The prefix shows which organization received the range.

sections.title: Examples, Security, and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC's example says an organization assigned 192.0.2.0/24 can use multicast address 234.192.0.2. An organization with a /16 can use a corresponding /24 multicast range and allocate addresses within it by its chosen method.

The RFC says familiar intra-domain security methods apply. Dynamic allocation within a smaller prefix may reduce the area where nodes compete for addresses. IANA assigned a /8 of global IPv4 multicast space for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how a unicast prefix leads to a multicast range. The RFC reserves a block for the method and notes that smaller allocation areas may limit competition.

references.text: Meyer, D. and P. Lothberg, "GLOP Addressing in 233/8", BCP 53, RFC 3180, September 2001.
